Subject:  Capital Improvement Program (CIP) Overview

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Review and comment on the City of Malibu's Capital Improvement
Program (CIP) including funding sources, project priorities, current challenges, and the
future CIP planning and budget process.

DISCUSSION: The Public Works Department manages the City’s Capital Improvement
Program (CIP) through coordination with City departments and external agencies. The
CIP provides a framework for planning, prioritizing, funding, and implementing capital
projects that maintain essential infrastructure, enhance public safety, support disaster
recovery, resilience and sustainability, and improve community use and modernization of
City facilities. Projects ultimately proceed subject to City Council approval and direction,
ensuring alignment with the City’s priorities and available funding.

Since incorporation in 1991, the City has invested in 38 facility improvements, 35 traffic
safety enhancements, three new parks, 20 sustainability and resilience projects, and 24
disaster response projects.

CIP Funding Sources
CIP projects are funded through the General Fund and a combination of one-time and
ongoing local, regional, State, and other funding sources, including:

  • Safe Clean Water Program (Measure W)
  • Proposition C - Local Return

  Page 1 of 2
  Agenda Item # 1.A.
   •  Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Act (RMRA)
  •  Measure M and R Local Return
  •  Community Development Block Grant (CDBG)
  •  Measure M - Subregional Highway Program
  •  Measure R - Highway Operational Improvements
  •  CA Joint Powers Insurance Authority (JPIA)
  •  Surface Transportation Program (STP) – Local
  •  Emergency Response Projects Funding
  •  Speed Safety Program (New Funding Source)
  •  General Fund
  •  Other Funding Sources

Current CIP funding allocations total approximately $14.1 million, distributed as follows:

  •  Stormwater Measure W – 4% ($491,300)
  •  Local Transportation Funding – 9% ($1.3 million)
  •  Regional Transportation Funding –39% (5.5 million)
  •  General Fund – 48% ($6.8 million)

Measure R approved by voters in 2008, expires in 2039, while Measure M approved in
2016, has no sunset date. To date, the City has received approximately $40.7 million in
Measure R funding and approximately $15.5 million in Measure M funding. These funds
have supported numerous traffic safety projects including:

  •  Park and Ride Land Purchase
  •  PCH at Trancas Canyon
  •  PCH Median Improvements
  •  PCH Signal Synchronization
  •  PCH at Las Flores Canyon and Rambla Pacifico
  •  Big Rock Pedestrian Crosswalk

Each September, staff submit eligible projects to Metro funding for consideration.
Following Metro Board approval in January, approved projects are incorporated into the
City's upcoming CIP budget.

In September 2026, staff requested that the annual Measure M allocation of $2 million be
applied to the Busch Drive Roundabouts project. During the upcoming budget process,
staff will seek Council direction on projects to submit to Metro in September 2027.

Impacts of Disasters
Since incorporation, Malibu has experienced 22 disasters, including one earthquake, 13
storms, 7 firestorms, and 1 global pandemic. These events have resulted in approximately
  Page 2 of 3
  Agenda Item # 1.A.
 $30 million in City expenditures since 2018, with approximately $9 million reimbursed by
FEMA and CalOES.

Staff continue to manage 4 active disasters involving FEMA and CalOES coordination and
reimbursement. Disaster response requires significant financial and staff resources, often
redirecting efforts from ongoing or planned capital project work to urgent public health and
safety needs.

FEMA and CalOES reimbursement processes require extensive documentation,
regulatory compliance, and coordination. Reimbursement requests can extend up to 9
years and may only cover a portion of eligible expenditures, create long-term financial
impacts, and reduce opportunities to invest available funds.

Future challenges, including severe storms (El Niño), sea level rise, coastal erosion,
climate change, and fires will continue to influence CIP priorities and resource allocation.

Current Project Status
The FY 2026-2027 CIP Program includes transportation and traffic safety projects,
recovery and wastewater projects, resiliency and sustainability projects, community and
cultural amenities, and initiatives focused on modernization. These projects support the
goals and objectives of the City’s Strategic Plan.

Staff will continue providing quarterly CIP updates to the City Council and monthly updates
to the PW Commission. Attachment 1 provides a comprehensive summary of active

Infrastructure Management and Maintenance:
The Public Works Department oversees multiple capital improvement projects
simultaneously, with responsibilities that include:

  • Conducting site visits, field inspections, and construction oversight
  • Coordinating with City departments, contractors, stakeholders, and external
  agencies
  • Addressing project-related issues, unforeseen conditions, and emergencies
  • Ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements, applicable codes, funding
  agreements, project specifications, and approved plans
  • Verifying construction quality through inspections, testing, and review of project
  submittals
  • Managing contracts, maintaining project records, and monitoring budgets and
  schedules
  • Verifying project completion, resolving outstanding items, and coordinating project
  acceptance and closeout

Proactive maintenance is essential to extending infrastructure lifespan and reducing long-
term costs. Maintenance needs vary based on asset type, age, condition, and operational
demands. The Department’s infrastructure management responsibilities include
maintaining asset inventories, assessing infrastructure conditions, prioritizing repairs and
replacements, and planning preventative maintenance activities. These efforts help
identify infrastructure needs and inform future CIP recommendations.

Infrastructure includes City facilities, streets, sidewalks, pathways, curbs and gutters,
bridges, traffic signals, parks, wastewater and recycled water facilities, stormwater
treatment facilities, and storm drain systems. Routine inspections, timely repairs, and

  Page 4 of 5
  Agenda Item # 1.A.
 readily available maintenance contracts help maintain safe and reliable infrastructure,
reduce likelihood of costly emergency repairs, and protect the City’s capital investments.

Future CIP recommendations will also identify anticipated operations and maintenance
costs, including staffing, utilities, contracted services, and eventual rehabilitation or
replacement. Incorporating these costs into project planning will help City Council with
decisions regarding the long-term financial commitments.

Council's Role in the CIP Budget Process
The Public Works Department uses planning documents, technical / engineering studies,
and community needs assessments to identify and prioritize projects. These resources
include:

  •  City of Malibu Strategic Plan 2025-2028
  •  City of Malibu General Plan
  •  City of Malibu Parks and Recreation Master Plan
  •  Recovery Needs Assessment – Palisades Fire
  •  Pacific Coast Highway Safety Study
  •  Storm Drain Master Plan
  •  Malibu Canyon Road Safety Study

At the January 2027 Council Workshop, Council will review and update the strategic
priorities that will be used to guide future CIP investments. Additionally, during the March
2027 Budget Workshop, staff will seek direction on:

  • FY 2027-2028 CIP Program Budget.
  • FY 2028-2029 Measure M projects to be submitted to Metro in September 2027.
  • FY 2028-2032 5-year Capital Plan.

This process will align project priorities with available funding, staffing resources, and the
City’s long-term infrastructure needs.

Future of the CIP Program
The future of the Capital Program is dependent on available funding, staffing, and
competing infrastructure priorities. To increase transparency, financial planning, and
project delivery, staff recommends updating the City’s five-year CIP Plan annually,
beginning with the existing FY 2023-2028 Plan.

Beginning in FY 2027-2028, the City anticipates approximately $4.5 million annual
revenue from the Speed Safety Camera Program authorized under Senate Bill 1297
(SB1297). Per SB1297, revenues will first be applied to recover implementation and

  Page 5 of 6
  Agenda Item # 1.A.
 operating costs. Excess revenue is restricted to traffic calming measures on PCH but
cannot replace existing spending commitments.

In the upcoming CIP budget process, Council may also provide direction on capital
projects involving Community Lands.

Moving forward, the CIP will continue to emphasize infrastructure resilience, sustainability,
modernization, public safety, and disaster recovery while balancing available resources
with community priorities.
